awd_titl_txt: Participant Support for Biomechanics Career Kickstarter Award for the 2025 American Society of Biomechanics Annual Meeting; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; 13-16 August 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant provides support for participant costs to develop two new initiatives during the 2025 American Society of Biomechanics Annual Meeting to be held in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 13-16 August 2025. 1) Develop a travel award called the “Biomechanics Career Kickstarter Award.” This award will prioritize first-time attendees and undergraduate students. 2) Speakers will be recruited to provide pre-conference webinars and workshops. Students who are typically unable to attend professional conferences will primarily benefit. The scientific meeting will contain biomechanics programming including keynote talks, oral presentations, and poster presentations. The meeting will also include activities to enable informal scientific discussions. The expected outcomes for the awardees will be career development through stronger scientific and networking skills. This meeting will enable workforce development that serves the biomechanics and health research community.
 
The new “Biomechanics Career Kickstarter Award” will be awarded to 10 applicants so that they can attend the 2025 American Society of Biomechanics Annual Meeting. The conference highlights and disseminates research across engineering biomechanics and mechanobiology, about the development and evaluation of rehabilitation engineering technologies, and research that integrates across intent, motor output, and technology. An advertising strategy will reach potential applicants beyond the society’s current community. Sites with “research experience for undergraduate” programs and regional meetings associated with the American Society of Biomechanics will expand the applicant pool beyond regular attendees. Programming (mentorship, webinars, and workshops) will prepare awardees for attending a scientific conference and ease their path into the society community. A workshop will focus on networking skills and pre-conference webinars will enable awardees to plan for the meeting. Evaluations will measure the impact of programming on attendees and on the awards on awardees. Dissemination will include a scientific abstract reporting the impacts of our evaluations. This meeting will provide awardees with a first step towards a career in biomechanics and enrich our understanding on how travel awards and professional development programming influences students’ ability to benefit from scientific meetings.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Attending a national scientific conference can be a turning point for a young researcher by connecting them with future mentors, collaborators, and career opportunities. But conferences are expensive, and students who are not part of well-funded research groups often cannot attend. This project addressed that gap at the 2025 American Society of Biomechanics Annual Meeting in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Through the Biomechanics Career Kickstarter Award, the project provided travel funding to students who typically face the greatest barriers to participation: undergraduates, first-time conference attendees, and students from institutions that are not research intensive. Interest was high, with 10 awardees selected from more than 100 applications. Selection prioritized applicants facing the most significant economic and institutional barriers.

A central idea of the project was that money alone may not be enough. Awardees therefore took part in pre-conference programming that prepared them to present their research, plan their conference schedule, and network effectively, along with a mentorship program that paired them with experienced attendees.

The results were strong. Awardees reported high satisfaction with the conference, averaging 4.78 out of 5. Nearly all reported that they met or exceeded their top personal goals, which centered on building professional networks, pursuing career opportunities, and improving their biomechanics knowledge. Surveys taken before and after the meeting showed significant gains in the specific skills targeted by the programming.

For conference skills that were not addressed by any program, students reported little to no improvement. This finding carries a clear lesson: simply attending a conference is not enough to build these skills on its own. Pairing financial support with intentional, targeted training produces better outcomes than either would alone.

Intellectual Merit: The project adds to a growing understanding of how early-career scientists develop, and it demonstrates a practical, measurable model for helping them succeed in the context of scientific conferences. These results build on findings from the prior year and will be shared with the wider research community through a presentation at the 2026 World Congress of Biomechanics in Vancouver, Canada.

The broader impacts extend beyond the individual awardees. By lowering the financial and social barriers that keep talented students out of scientific communities, the project helped widen the pool of people who can contribute to biomechanics and related fields. Awardees gained connections, confidence, and skills that will follow them throughout their careers. Furthermore, the project offers a replicable approach that other conferences and scientific societies can adopt to make their communities more welcoming, more diverse, and more accessible to the next generation of scientists.
